"Dispersing the surface" referred to induced sweating, a therapy designed to expel excessive Heat. Like many "Danxi" pronouncements, this one was assembled in the fifteenth century from fragments that had also appeared in the Jingui gouxuan 金匱鉤玄 (late 14th century) and its likely predecessor, a manuscript that was published in 1475 under the title Danxi michuan fangjue 丹溪密傳方訣. See Jingui gouxuan, juan 1, "Shui zhong" 水腫 (Danxi yiji: 99; this passage does not appear in the SKQS ed.): "after childbirth, one must chiefly use massive replenishing of Blood and Qi" (產後必用大補氣血為主); and 3.11b, "Furen ke" 婦人科, "Fa re wu han" 發熱惡寒 (Danxi yiji: 122): "peonies cannot be given postpartum because their acidity and cooling [properties] destroy vital Qi. Dispersing must not be used [to treat] any postpartum disorder." (產後不可下白芍以其酸寒伐生發之氣故也 產後一切病皆不可發散) The first editor of the Danxi xinfa in the 1450s, a man named Yang Xun 楊珣, compiled these passages in his effort to reconstruct Zhu Zhenheng's approach to postpartum problems. See Yang's Danxi xinfa, sec. 102, "Postpartum" 產後, in juan 4 (Liu and Xue 2005: 301). More on the Xinfa and its editions in 5.5. Earlier remarks by Liu Chun 劉純 contained a key difference from the wording of the Danxi xinfa. "Our Danxi xiansheng said that if there are no noxious blockers (如無惡阻) postpartum, one should massively replenish Qi and Blood, and that even if there are other symptoms, they should be treated as offshoots" (Yuji weiji 玉機微義 [1396] 49.58a [LiuYChQ: 436B]. Liu probably copied these instructions from notes or manuscripts, since some of these phrases appeared in Danxi michuan fangjue 丹溪秘傳方訣 (HWHG 5: 210-13). It could be that Yang Xun, who was from Xi'an, read the 1439 edition of Liu's Yuji weiji (which was also made in Xi'an), but his version of Danxi's claims on postpartum disorders was nonetheless cruder than Liu's. The Huizhou editors of the Xinfa simply recopied the resulting sentence from Yang's recension. Zhu's more complex instructions on how a woman who had just given birth should be treated (from Jufang fabui 局方發揮 1.28b; Danxi yiji: 46) were rarely cited. An exception was Lou Ying's Yixue gangmu 醫學綱目 [1396, first printed in 1565] (juan 35, "Chanhou zheng" 產後癥; 1996 [1396]: 811A).

All of these men had read the Danxi xinfa 丹溪心法 (1482), knew of Wang Lun's 王綸 (1453-1510) arguments on Yin-replenishing, and embraced a syncretistic approach to past medical teachings. In the domain that interests us, the main event of the sixteenth century was perhaps the re-definition of dian 癲 as a form of madness characterized by non-manic symptoms and best treated by replenishing. The illness dian had existed since at least the third century BCE, and it had been associated with kuang since the first century BCE, but its main symptoms had first been close to those of epilepsy. They were Xu Xianqing 徐顯卿 (jinshi 1568, became Vice-Minister of Personnel, rank 3a) and Wu Shaoxi 吴少溪 (his hao), a former Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent (also ranked 3a). Theirs are cases 1, 4, 25, 29, 36, 37, 39, 40 of the Yixing 宜興 section of Sun's collection (Sunshi yian 孫氏醫案, juan 5). In 1597, Xu Xianqing wrote a preface to Sun's Chishui xuanzhu 赤水玄珠 (SunYQ: 4) soon after he had been cured by Sun, whom he had met almost two decades earlier (see cases 1 [1579], 29 [undated], 36 [1581], and 39 [1598]; in SunYQ: 827-28, 833A, 834-35, and 836AB). Sun also treated magistrate Hu Jingyang 胡鏡陽 and his family members (cases 5, 7, and 35; in SunYQ: 828B-29A, 829B, and 834A) and a magistrate surnamed Song 宋 from Shandong (case 3; SunYQ: 828B). $ ^{93} $ Sun went to Yixing from Huzhou in late 1597 and in the spring of 1598, and returned directly to Huzhou (which he called Tiao 苕 after the name of a local river). Late 1597 visit and return to Huzhou soon after the New Year: Yixing, case 37 (SunYQ: 835); arrival in the spring of 1598: case 2 (828); presence in Yixing in the late summer 1598: cases 39 and 40 (836-7); return to Huzhou in the fall of 1598: case 38 (835-6). Cases 1 and 2 (dated 1574), and case 3 (1577) in the San-Wu section (SunYQ: 735-36) show that Sun was in Huzhou in the 1570's.

Wang Wenbi's 汪文壁 preface to Sun's casebook (SunYQ: 709) explained that it was Huzhou gentry who had encouraged Sun to print his case files in a joint edition with Sun's two other books, (discussed below). Four of the five "Texts bestowed by illustrious local gentry" (諸縉紳名家贈文; SunYQ: 714-18) that appeared at the beginning of Sun's case collection were authored by Huzhou men, who called their native place Gui'an 歸安, Wuxing 吳興, or Xi Wu 西吳. The three dated texts were from 1573 (1) and 1576 (2). The 1573 text by Grand Coordinator (大中丞; ranked 2a) Shen Tong 沈桐 mentioned that Sun, who already enjoyed a good reputation at the time, was then beginning to travel in Huzhou (SunYQ: 716). Sun's collection is often dated to 1573 on the basis of its earliest "preface" (xu序), but the book's earliest dated case is from 1574, and I mentioned cases from 1598 in the previous note. The texts bestowed by Huzhou notables did not mention any book by Sun. A xu could indeed commemorate an occasion regardless of whether a book was being published.

As an edition of the Jinhua prefectural gazetteer (“examinations”科第; cited in Danxi yijr: 704) recorded, only one candidate from Wuzhou passed the provincial examination in 1320.   "chapter_body_excerpt": "## 4 ## From Wind to mucus and Fire The innovations of Jin and Yuan physicians, ca. 1150-1360 In Chapter 3, I traced the increasingly widespread association of mucus with Wind disorders from the tenth to the twelfth century and showed that several illnesses whose pathomechanisms had been considered close to those of kuang—Wind strokes and xian 痈 seizures—were often treated with anti-mucus remedies by the end of that period. Let me now explain how the mucus-and-Fire etiology of madness that dominated late-imperial conceptions of insanity developed. The mucus-and-Fire script emerged among doctrinally minded physicians who lived in north China under the Jin dynasty (1115-1234), and was consolidated by southern doctors who were influenced by these northerners in the early fourteenth century under the Yuan dynasty (1260-1368), after the Mongol conquest of both the Jin and the southern Song (1127-1279) had re-established contacts between north and south China. The innovations these medical thinkers proposed built on the trends I outlined in Chapter 3, but it was their doctrinal and therapeutic precepts that came to dominate later medical thinking. During these men's lives (and partly thanks to their efforts), \"Cold Injury\" (shangban 傷寒) replaced \"Wind illnesses\" as the new dominant class of illnesses. The way Jin-Yuan physicians interpreted madness and handled mad people depended on their broader understanding of illness and vitality.   "chapter_body_excerpt": "## Shapes of practice Medical trends surrounding dian and kuang, 17th-19th century The profusion of medical works that appeared after 1650 are an irritating windfall. As medical publications boomed, vectors of knowledge transmission and the doctrinal debates that interested physicians became more intricate and numerous. It thus becomes difficult to find narrative threads to explain how Qing medical reflections on madness changed. Far too many texts were published for me to base my conclusions on comprehensive data as I tried to do for earlier periods. But the extensive array of short treatises, collections of case files, formularies, and medical primers that appeared in Qing times hint to the thinking and practice of minor physicians who made no “contributions to the development of Chinese medicine”—to borrow a phrase from a less critical historiography. These works allow us to see how much medical luminaries had in common with their less famous counterparts. I first present a few important trends in Chinese medical thinking and practice from the seventeenth to the nineteenth century. After showing that the mucus etiology remained dominant over that period, I show how resilient and ubiquitous the script of blockage of the Heart by mucus was. I map the vivid “imagination of mucus” $ ^{1} $ through which physicians—from treatise writers to village healers—continued to envision madness from the seventeenth to the nineteenth century. I then turn to a pivotal figure in eighteenth-century medicine—Ye Gui 葉桂 (1667-1746)—and to what an influential work attributed to him said about madness. Ming and Qing physicians cited these sayings to set up concurring arguments, to introduce objections or qualifications, or to clinch points with the help of a well-formulated piece of common knowledge. In this chapter, I want to explore whether the gender of the sufferer was one of the fault lines along which the understanding and treatment of mad acts and mad people were divided. Did physicians from the Song (960-1279) to the Qing (1644-1911) describe madness as occurring to women by different mechanisms than to men? Did the treatments they prescribed differ according to the gender of the patient? What other aspects of medical approaches to insanity were “gendered”? Since mad behavior was obviously less frequent than menses and pregnancy, relatively few cases of madness where the patient was a woman have survived.   "chapter_body_excerpt": "## 12 Punish, but how? Mad acts and their punishments, 1750-1911 Chapter 11 explained why most killings committed because of insanity between 1669 and 1750 were sentenced under a law called “killing because of madness,” which requested that killers pay a monetary compensation to the family of their victims. In the second half of the eighteenth century, however, death sentences became common for the same acts, while ever stricter measures of preventive confinement were imposed on “people with madness illness.” By 1850, nine sub-statutes discussed mad homicides, and an increasing number of “circulars” (通行) and “memoranda” (説貼) from the Ministry of Punishments instructed legal officials on how to handle these crimes. Why were so many different punishments imposed for homicides that used to be sentenced in the same way until the 1750s? The diverse sentences meted out for killings committed “because of madness” did not reflect Chinese ambiguities about the criminal responsibility of mad people, but changing assessments of the justness of sentencing in specific cases. Although the legal view of mad acts did not change, the insanity of killers was no longer the only circumstance deemed relevant to sentencing. The diversity of punishments resulted from unsystematic attempts by Qing officials to impose severe punishments for acts that led to grave outcomes, and to maintain equilibrium between the penalties required for proximate crimes. Some of these balancing efforts created new discrepancies that required further tweaking. $ ^{1} $ I first clarify the legislative and judicial importance of preserving the right balance between criminal acts and their punishments, and of grading punishments between crimes that the Code treated as proximate.   "chapter_body_excerpt": "I noted in Chapter 1 that Martha Li Chiu (1986) scoured the Inner Canon to find a Chinese medical object comparable to mental illness, and that she settled on kuang because it was mostly characterized by \"mental symptoms.\" But by describing symptoms (rather than illnesses) as either mental or physical, she reproduced a problematic dichotomy at a lower level without uncovering the assumptions it hides. Below, I propose an alternative way of comparing Chinese medical approaches with psychiatric ones. My goal is to foster our understanding of medical discourse on kuang by breaking free from the preconceptions that lurk beneath the notions of \"mental\" and \"physical.\" ### 3.2 Psycho-behavioral pathology in Chinese medicine Comparisons: why not “mental illness”? Most scholars (Chinese and Western alike) who have written on insanity in Chinese history since the 1950s have used the phrase “mental illness” either to describe their object or to pose this notion as the basis for comparing psychiatry with Chinese medicine. $ ^{14} $ But the pure notion of “mental illness” with which Chinese conceptions are so often contrasted (or deemed incomparable) may never have existed. From the era of “mad-doctoring” to the latest edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (or DSM; see APA 1994), behavioral symptoms have been at the center of psychiatric attention. The preconception that the notion “mental illness” depends on a mind-body dualism has also hindered comparisons.   "chapter_body_excerpt": "“Danxi said…” The textual life of medical ideas on madness, 1360-1530 Danxi said that dian belongs to Yin and kuang to Yang, that dian is excessive joy and kuang excessive anger. He also stated that the doubling of Yin is dian and the doubling of Yang is kuang. 丹溪謂癲屬陰 狂屬陽 癲多喜 狂多怒 又云重陰者癲 重陽者狂 Xu Chunfu 徐春甫 in Gujin yitong daquan 古今醫統大全 (1556) $ ^{1} $ Chapters 3 and 4 traced a momentous transformation in the etiology of madness from Wind to internal Fire and mucus between the twelfth and the fourteenth century. The Ming dynasty (1368-1644) was not a period of strong epistemological breaks in medicine, but one in which physicians re-orchestrated earlier approaches to form new doctrinal and therapeutic emphases. Xu Chunfu above was citing the Danxi xinfa 丹溪心法, a composite work compiled and printed in his own Huizhou Prefecture (Anhui) in the early 1480s and that quickly became the most influential work attributed to Zhu Zhenheng 朱震亨 (\"Danxi\" 丹溪: 1282-1358). This and the next chapter show how the development of Ming medical thinking on dian and kuang was shaped by three important trends that are well symbolized by Xu's quotation: the rising influence of precepts attributed to Danxi, the importance of Huizhou as a center of medical theorizing and publication, and the profound intertextuality of the elite medical tradition. ### 5.1 Intertextual composition and the Danxi corpus The “Danxi corpus” in the history of medical thinking on madness The rise to prominence of a body of teachings attributed to Zhu Zhenheng deeply shaped Ming medical thinking and practice. Zhu's teachings appeared in a wide array of texts books and manuscripts by Zhu, notes by his disciples, works attributed to Zhu that were collated after his death by people who had known him, and later anthologies base ..."

  "chapter_body_excerpt": "## Shapes of practice Medical trends surrounding dian and kuang, 17th-19th century The profusion of medical works that appeared after 1650 are an irritating windfall. As medical publications boomed, vectors of knowledge transmission and the doctrinal debates that interested physicians became more intricate and numerous. It thus becomes difficult to find narrative threads to explain how Qing medical reflections on madness changed. Far too many texts were published for me to base my conclusions on comprehensive data as I tried to do for earlier periods. But the extensive array of short treatises, collections of case files, formularies, and medical primers that appeared in Qing times hint to the thinking and practice of minor physicians who made no “contributions to the development of Chinese medicine”—to borrow a phrase from a less critical historiography. These works allow us to see how much medical luminaries had in common with their less famous counterparts. I first present a few important trends in Chinese medical thinking and practice from the seventeenth to the nineteenth century. After showing that the mucus etiology remained dominant over that period, I show how resilient and ubiquitous the script of blockage of the Heart by mucus was. I map the vivid “imagination of mucus” $ ^{1} $ through which physicians—from treatise writers to village healers—continued to envision madness from the seventeenth to the nineteenth century. I then turn to a pivotal figure in eighteenth-century medicine—Ye Gui 葉桂 (1667-1746)—and to what an influential work attributed to him said about madness. As medical publications boomed, vectors of knowledge transmission and the doctrinal debates that interested physicians became more intricate and numerous. Far too many texts were published for me to base my conclusions on comprehensive data as I tried to do for earlier periods. In addition to writing long sections on diankuang in their treatises, physicians from this ebullient period recorded in some detail how they handled specific cases of madness. All of these men had read the Danxi xinfa 丹溪心法 (1482), knew of Wang Lun's 王綸 (1453-1510) arguments on Yin-replenishing, and embraced a syncretistic approach to past medical teachings. Their clinical practice and most of the doctrinal debates in which they engaged were thus informed by the trends in medical thinking that I described in previous chapters. In the domain that interests us, the main event of the sixteenth century was perhaps the re-definition of dian 癲 as a form of madness characterized by non-manic symptoms and best treated by replenishing. The illness dian had existed since at least the third century BCE, and it had been associated with kuang since the first century BCE, but its main symptoms had first been close to those of epilepsy.   "chapter_body_excerpt": "## Shapes of practice Medical trends surrounding dian and kuang, 17th-19th century The profusion of medical works that appeared after 1650 are an irritating windfall. As medical publications boomed, vectors of knowledge transmission and the doctrinal debates that interested physicians became more intricate and numerous. It thus becomes difficult to find narrative threads to explain how Qing medical reflections on madness changed. Far too many texts were published for me to base my conclusions on comprehensive data as I tried to do for earlier periods. But the extensive array of short treatises, collections of case files, formularies, and medical primers that appeared in Qing times hint to the thinking and practice of minor physicians who made no “contributions to the development of Chinese medicine”—to borrow a phrase from a less critical historiography. These works allow us to see how much medical luminaries had in common with their less famous counterparts. I first present a few important trends in Chinese medical thinking and practice from the seventeenth to the nineteenth century. After showing that the mucus etiology remained dominant over that period, I show how resilient and ubiquitous the script of blockage of the Heart by mucus was.   "chapter_body_excerpt": "“Danxi said…” The textual life of medical ideas on madness, 1360-1530 Danxi said that dian belongs to Yin and kuang to Yang, that dian is excessive joy and kuang excessive anger. He also stated that the doubling of Yin is dian and the doubling of Yang is kuang. 丹溪謂癲屬陰 狂屬陽 癲多喜 狂多怒 又云重陰者癲 重陽者狂 Xu Chunfu 徐春甫 in Gujin yitong daquan 古今醫統大全 (1556) $ ^{1} $ Chapters 3 and 4 traced a momentous transformation in the etiology of madness from Wind to internal Fire and mucus between the twelfth and the fourteenth century. The Ming dynasty (1368-1644) was not a period of strong epistemological breaks in medicine, but one in which physicians re-orchestrated earlier approaches to form new doctrinal and therapeutic emphases. Xu Chunfu above was citing the Danxi xinfa 丹溪心法, a composite work compiled and printed in his own Huizhou Prefecture (Anhui) in the early 1480s and that quickly became the most influential work attributed to Zhu Zhenheng 朱震亨 (\"Danxi\" 丹溪: 1282-1358). This and the next chapter show how the development of Ming medical thinking on dian and kuang was shaped by three important trends that are well symbolized by Xu's quotation: the rising influence of precepts attributed to Danxi, the importance of Huizhou as a center of medical theorizing and publication, and the profound intertextuality of the elite medical tradition. ### 5.1 Intertextual composition and the Danxi corpus The “Danxi corpus” in the history of medical thinking on madness The rise to prominence of a body of teachings attributed to Zhu Zhenheng deeply shaped Ming medical thinking and practice. matched_examples.anchor_excerpt: Yongwen mubiao”蔣公用文墓表 [1424], in Yang's Dongli wenji 東里文集 [1440] 16.20b-22b. 71 Yang's preface to Yuji weiji 玉機微義 ended by praising Chen Yi for diffusing medical teachings, as medicine was “the art by which the sages display benevolence upon the people” (醫者聖人仁民之術也; LiuChYQ: 73). History of the Ming (138: 4137) indicates that in the early Zhengtong reign (in or soon after 1436), Yang “dispatched military and civil officials to zhenfu Jiangxi, Huguang, Henan, and Shandong” (分遣文武鎮撫江西湖廣 河南 山東). Yang was probably the one who sent Chen to Shaanxi in 1435. John Dardess (1996: 179-89) discussed Yang's patronizing of natives of Taihe, but said little about his relations with other court officials. 72 LiuChYQ: 463. In 1438 Yang Shiqi had been named Junior Preceptor (少師), a prestige title ranked 1b. Duxian 都憲 is not listed in Hucker 1985, but it probably referred to a post in the Censorate. A sample mistake in Chen's edition: “Wang Andao” 王安道 (Zhu's disciple Wang Liu) was turned into “Yu'an daoren” 玉安道人 (“Taoist master Yu'an”; juan 1, “Wind strokes,” “neiyin si zhongfeng lun” 内因似中風論; LiuChYQ: 117A). 73 Angela Leung (2003b: 132) postulated that Yang's writing a preface for it showed that the Yijing xianxue 醫經小學 was “an important introductory textbook during the early Ming,” but it appears that Yang's preface enabled rather than recognized the influence of this text.

History of the Ming (138: 4137) indicates that in the early Zhengtong reign (in or soon after 1436), Yang “dispatched military and civil officials to zhenfu Jiangxi, Huguang, Henan, and Shandong” (分遣文武鎮撫江西湖廣 河南 山東). Yang was probably the one who sent Chen to Shaanxi in 1435. John Dardess (1996: 179-89) discussed Yang's patronizing of natives of Taihe, but said little about his relations with other court officials. 72 LiuChYQ: 463. In 1438 Yang Shiqi had been named Junior Preceptor (少師), a prestige title ranked 1b. Duxian 都憲 is not listed in Hucker 1985, but it probably referred to a post in the Censorate. A sample mistake in Chen's edition: “Wang Andao” 王安道 (Zhu's disciple Wang Liu) was turned into “Yu'an daoren” 玉安道人 (“Taoist master Yu'an”; juan 1, “Wind strokes,” “neiyin si zhongfeng lun” 内因似中風論; LiuChYQ: 117A). 73 Angela Leung (2003b: 132) postulated that Yang's writing a preface for it showed that the Yijing xianxue 醫經小學 was “an important introductory textbook during the early Ming,” but it appears that Yang's preface enabled rather than recognized the influence of this text.

  "chapter_body_excerpt": "## Shapes of practice Medical trends surrounding dian and kuang, 17th-19th century The profusion of medical works that appeared after 1650 are an irritating windfall. As medical publications boomed, vectors of knowledge transmission and the doctrinal debates that interested physicians became more intricate and numerous. It thus becomes difficult to find narrative threads to explain how Qing medical reflections on madness changed. Far too many texts were published for me to base my conclusions on comprehensive data as I tried to do for earlier periods. But the extensive array of short treatises, collections of case files, formularies, and medical primers that appeared in Qing times hint to the thinking and practice of minor physicians who made no “contributions to the development of Chinese medicine”—to borrow a phrase from a less critical historiography. These works allow us to see how much medical luminaries had in common with their less famous counterparts. I first present a few important trends in Chinese medical thinking and practice from the seventeenth to the nineteenth century. After showing that the mucus etiology remained dominant over that period, I show how resilient and ubiquitous the script of blockage of the Heart by mucus was. I map the vivid “imagination of mucus” $ ^{1} $ through which physicians—from treatise writers to village healers—continued to envision madness from the seventeenth to the nineteenth century.   "chapter_body_excerpt": "# 11 Errors and projections The emergence of “madness” in Qing law, 1654-1750 Because they are produced in concrete and particular social relations, the meaning and the materiality of law are inseparable. $ ^{1} $ Previous scholarship on Qing madness laws has largely focused on the question of the “criminal responsibility” of mad people, in reference to an early scholarly debate: in riposte to an adverse review (van der Valk 1948) of his annotated translation (Bünger 1946) of important legal texts, Karl Bünger (1903-1997) maintained that “the exemption of lunatics from punishment [.... has been] a principle of the Chinese law from the Zhou dynasty until nowadays” (Bünger 1950: 8-9). This argument, based chiefly on two texts separated by more than a millennium, can be disproved with counter-examples. $ ^{2} $ More serious is the fact that even refutations have not significantly modified Bünger’s framework. Nakamura Shigeo (1973d), Martha Li Chiu (1981), Vivien Ng (1980, 1984, and 1990), and Erhard Rosner (1991) have all implied that the way the Qing legal system treated insane offenders was the system’s approach to the problem of their “criminal responsibility.” As I shall show, Qing laws that mentioned insanity applied only to killings and were not based on any principle that defined responsibility at large.   "chapter_body_excerpt": "## Shapes of practice Medical trends surrounding dian and kuang, 17th-19th century The profusion of medical works that appeared after 1650 are an irritating windfall. As medical publications boomed, vectors of knowledge transmission and the doctrinal debates that interested physicians became more intricate and numerous. It thus becomes difficult to find narrative threads to explain how Qing medical reflections on madness changed. Far too many texts were published for me to base my conclusions on comprehensive data as I tried to do for earlier periods. But the extensive array of short treatises, collections of case files, formularies, and medical primers that appeared in Qing times hint to the thinking and practice of minor physicians who made no “contributions to the development of Chinese medicine”—to borrow a phrase from a less critical historiography. These works allow us to see how much medical luminaries had in common with their less famous counterparts. I first present a few important trends in Chinese medical thinking and practice from the seventeenth to the nineteenth century. After showing that the mucus etiology remained dominant over that period, I show how resilient and ubiquitous the script of blockage of the Heart by mucus was. I map the vivid “imagination of mucus” $ ^{1} $ through which physicians—from treatise writers to village healers—continued to envision madness from the seventeenth to the nineteenth century. I then turn to a pivotal figure in eighteenth-century medicine—Ye Gui 葉桂 (1667-1746)—and to what an influential work attributed to him said about madness.   "chapter_body_excerpt": "## 2 Prologue to Part One Diversity, coherence, and scheme transfer Medicine is the most complex field I shall be studying. Qing legislative and judicial practices were far from simple, but criminal trials followed common procedures and referred to a single body of laws that discussed madness and mad acts with consistent terminology. Although Qing laws were often modified, officials worked with only one code. Medical texts form a less cohesive corpus.   "chapter_body_excerpt": "## 16 ## Madness multiple $ ^{1} $ Language, illness, and behavior in law and medicine Madness is not an entity or an essence, but an ascribed characteristic of various acts, words, or people. In practice—while treating an illness, judging a legal case, or taking care of a sick relative at home—people could label specific men or women, acts or words, as being diankuang 癫狂, fengdian 風顛, or fengbing 瘋病. But these labels were contextual. Several different words could thus be used to refer to the same person. Depending on what they wanted to emphasize, villagers could call a man's manic behavior kuang 狂, the oddness of his deportment dian 顛, his unrealistic aspirations chi 癡, or his more uncanny acts guai 怪. Conversely, two different terms did not have to refer to mutually exclusive realities. A woman in rural Henan, for instance, could easily accept that the legal category fengbing (“madness illness”) applied to her son even if she labeled him dian and considered him possessed. Even judicial reports used fengbing side by side with non-technical terms like fengdian 風癲 or medical expressions like “mucus confusing the openings of the Heart” 痰迷心竅 as if they were all equivalent. My focus on practical usage eased the problem of definitions, but even as I tried not to base my investigations on a universal, I had to struggle with how swiftly and easily Qing people—be it a man who sought medical treatment for his mad brother or an official who dealt with a homicide—identified insanity.
